fixes.explanation: It does. The very next line asks, "Why have You forgotten us forever? Why have You forsaken us for so long?" Those are the prayer's own words and its own question. It holds "You, O LORD, reign forever…" and that aching question side by side, and it doesn't hide either one.

That's the pair: "We submitted to Egypt and Assyria to get enough bread." Egypt and Assyria were two other nations. Bread was the reason the prayer gives. Getting enough of it is what the line is about.

A blessing isn't what the verse says. It says, "Our fathers sinned and are no more, but we bear their punishment." It's the punishment they bear, and it's a heavy line. The prayer says it out loud anyway.
Not quite, friend. The verse says, "…there is no one to deliver us from their hands." It says no one is there to deliver them, and it doesn't mention anyone on the way. It's a hard thing to say.
That's it, friend. The verse says, "…there is no one to deliver us from their hands." It says nothing about someone being on the way. It's a hard thing to say, and the prayer says it anyway.
Yes, "Our skin is as hot as an oven with fever from our hunger." The fever is the picture, and hunger is the cause the prayer names. It's another heavy line, so I'll just say that once.
Yes, "…Mount Zion, which lies desolate, patrolled by foxes." Desolate means empty and left behind. The prayer says their eyes grow dim because of Mount Zion. I think that's the heart of their grief.
The verse doesn't say that. It says, "…Mount Zion, which lies desolate, patrolled by foxes." Desolate is the word, and it means empty and left behind. Foxes are the ones patrolling it.

Yes! "You, O LORD, reign forever; Your throne endures from generation to generation." The prayer says this out loud right after naming all that loss. The throne is said to endure from generation to generation. That's a big turn in the prayer, friend.
